analysis.one_liner: Creates universal federally funded child care and early learning with family fees capped at 7% of income
analysis.headline: A bill to create universal child care, backed by 96 House Democrats, was referred to the Education and Workforce Committee in February 2023 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set up a universal child care and early learning program run through states, cities, tribes, and nonprofits, open to every child not yet in school regardless of family income, disability, or citizenship [S2]. Families below twice the poverty line would pay nothing, and no family would pay more than 7% of its income, with the federal government covering at least 90% of program costs [S2] [S3]. It also directed sponsors to set child care worker pay through a bargaining process with the workforce [S3]. The bill was referred to committee and never moved [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Families with young children, who today often pay $10,000 or more a year for care in many areas: the bill would have made care free for families under 200% of the poverty line and capped everyone else's fees on a sliding scale topping out at 7% of income [S2] [S3]. The program would run a full working day (at least 10 hours) and full calendar year, and guarantee every requesting family a placement, including children with disabilities, homeless children, and children of migrant farmworkers [S3]. Child care workers would gain, because sponsors had to set wages, benefits, and working conditions through a collective process with unions or staff representatives [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families with young children and child care workers

how_it_helps.text: Every child not yet required to attend school would be entitled to a slot in the program regardless of family income, disability status, or citizenship, and the entitlement is uncapped [S2] [S3].

Fees would be waived for families below 200% of the poverty line and capped at 7% of income for everyone else, charged on a sliding scale with no increase beyond that cap no matter how many children in the family are enrolled [S2] [S3].

The federal government would pay at least 90% of program costs (100% for tribal and migrant farmworker programs), and sponsors must serve every family that requests a placement, offering both center-based and home-based options [S3].

Sponsors would have to recognize and bargain with unions representing child care teachers and home-based providers, and pay compensation meeting federal wage requirements, addressing a workforce where pay is among the lowest in the economy [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through appropriations of 'such sums as may be necessary' for an uncapped entitlement with no total price attached to the bill [S3]. Middle- and higher-income families would pay sliding-scale fees up to 7% of income. States and localities would be barred from cutting their existing child care spending to offset the new federal money [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates 'such sums as may be necessary' for an uncapped entitlement covering every preschool-age child in the country, with no total cost estimate in the bill itself; a program of this scale would likely cost tens of billions of dollars a year, a price the bill leaves to future Congresses [S3].

Because eligibility is universal, federal subsidies would also flow to higher-income families, raising the total cost compared with targeting aid to families who cannot otherwise afford care [S2] [S3].

Providers, including small home-based caregivers, would have to meet new national program standards and collectively bargained wage floors; sponsors are required to ensure providers' operating costs are covered, but the transition could be difficult for small providers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to families is large and direct: child care is one of the biggest household expenses for parents of young children, and the bill attacks both the cost and the shortage of slots. The honest cost is fiscal scale — an uncapped, universal entitlement with no price tag in the bill, at a time when Congress was unwilling to pass even a scaled-back version. A cheaper, means-tested design would have cost far less; the universal structure was a deliberate choice to avoid a two-tier system, but it made the price harder to defend. The wage provisions are a real strength: raising child care worker pay without it tends to simply raise families' fees.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never held a hearing or voted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025 [S5].

narrative.text: Representative Mikie Sherrill introduced the Child Care for Every Community Act on February 9, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce [S1] [S5].
96 of the 216 House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsor appears in the record [S4].
The committee took no further action — no hearing, markup, or report — and the bill never reached the House floor; the full action history contains only the introduction and the referral [S5].
The bill expired with the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025, without either chamber ever voting on it [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Families with young children got no relief from child care costs. The parties better off because the bill died are child care providers who would have faced new national standards and union wage-setting, and federal taxpayers, who avoided the open-ended cost of a universal entitlement the bill never priced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Providers facing new mandates, and taxpayers

against.name: Chair Virginia Foxx
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred to her committee; it sat without action for two years.

against.name: 224 of 224 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Controlled the chamber's agenda; no Republican cosponsored the bill and it was never brought to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 96 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the bill died in the Republican-held committee without a hearing or vote.

industries.note: Public and private providers, including for-profit agencies and home-based caregivers, could serve as funded 'delegate providers' under the program, giving them a large new federal revenue stream; in exchange they would have to meet national quality standards and pay collectively bargained wages, which the federal share is required to cover [S3]. Families pay less while providers get paid — their interests point the same way in this bill.

industries.industry: Child care workers and their unions
industries.note: The bill required sponsors to bargain with unions or staff representatives over wages, benefits, and working conditions and to meet federal compensation requirements, directly targeting the sector's notoriously low pay [S3].

For-profit organizations could apply as delegate providers, but a heavily subsidized program charging families no more than 7% of income would draw enrollment away from full-price private care, shrinking their paying customer base while offering a lower-margin publicly funded contract alternative [S3].
